paragraphs: Generalization bounds describe how far a learning algorithm’s performance on training data can differ from its performance beyond those data. Several information-theoretic approaches address this question using different mathematical quantities. This paper develops a shared methodology that produces new bounds and recovers many established results within one framework.

Its central tool is a probabilistic decorrelation lemma. The lemma uses a change of probability measure and a relaxed form of Young’s inequality in particular Orlicz spaces. The authors combine it with symmetrization, couplings, and chaining over probability measures to obtain upper bounds both for average generalization error and for error with high probability.

The framework includes bounds based on mutual information, conditional mutual information, stochastic chaining, and PAC-Bayes inequalities as special cases. It also recovers the Fernique–Talagrand upper bound for the expected supremum of a subgaussian process. These connections make the contribution a unifying mathematical tool: seemingly separate guarantees can be derived through a common mechanism, alongside additional bounds.
neurips-2023-a-unified-framework-for-inf.tldr: A shared mathematical framework derives new information-theoretic generalization bounds and recovers many existing guarantees as special cases.

paragraphs: Integrated Multimodal Perception, or IMP, brings images, video, text, and audio into one Transformer encoder with few components dedicated to individual input types. The aim is to scale learning across both modalities and tasks while limiting conflicts between the different kinds of information the model must process.

IMP combines two design choices. Alternating Gradient Descent switches training updates across modalities, objectives, tasks, and input resolutions. A sparse mixture of experts adds specialized computation within the shared encoder. The empirical studies find that alternating updates improves learning efficiently, while the expert design improves performance over dense models with separate modality encoders or extra fusion layers.

The resulting models perform competitively on image and video classification and on retrieval involving text. A video-focused sparse model reaches reported zero-shot classification scores of 77.0%, 76.8%, and 68.3% on the three Kinetics benchmarks. It exceeds the previous best results while using 15% of their total training computation, supporting the efficiency of this combination in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2023-alternating-gradient-descen.tldr: IMP combines alternating training updates and sparse experts in one multimodal encoder, achieving strong results with substantially lower reported training computation.

paragraphs: An algorithm can predict more accurately than a human expert while still missing information that the expert uses. This paper asks how to detect that additional expertise, especially when human judgments draw on intuition or observations unavailable in the recorded data. Comparing accuracy with one particular algorithm cannot settle that question.

The authors formulate a statistical test of whether expert predictions and actual outcomes are independent after accounting for the available input features. If expert judgments still contain information about outcomes after this conditioning, the test can reject independence. Such a rejection suggests that experts may contribute value beyond what any predictor trained on those available features can capture.

Using emergency-department admissions data, the authors find that physicians’ decisions for patients with acute gastrointestinal bleeding appear to incorporate information unavailable to a standard screening tool. This occurs even though the tool is arguably more accurate overall. The result explains why aggregate accuracy alone is insufficient to justify automation and why testing for additional information matters when assessing possible human–AI complementarity.
neurips-2023-auditing-for-human-expertis.tldr: A conditional-independence test assesses whether human judgments contain useful information beyond an algorithm’s available features, even when the algorithm is more accurate.

paragraphs: Bridge3D investigates how knowledge from foundation models for images and language can improve representations of three-dimensional scenes. Those models already provide useful features, object masks, and descriptions, but differences between their domains and 3D data make transferring that knowledge difficult. The paper uses these outputs together during 3D pretraining.

One component uses semantic masks to guide which information a masked autoencoder hides and reconstructs, concentrating learning on foreground representations. Another uses image captions to transfer knowledge about entire scenes into the 3D model. A further object-level distillation component combines accurate object masks with semantic text, providing guidance at a more localized scale.

These components connect visual structure and language to 3D learning at both scene and object levels. The authors report substantial improvements over existing methods on 3D object detection and semantic segmentation, including a 6.3% improvement over a baseline on ScanNet. The findings support using foundation-model outputs as structured pretraining signals for 3D understanding, rather than treating their usefulness as confined to image or language tasks.
neurips-2023-bridging-the-domain-gap-sel.tldr: Bridge3D uses foundation-model masks, features, and captions to improve 3D pretraining through foreground reconstruction and scene- and object-level knowledge transfer.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in a video requires understanding both what appears in individual frames and how the scene changes over time. The paper argues that many action-recognition models do not balance these two demands well. CAST addresses this with separate spatial and temporal expert models that work together using RGB video input.

The key connection between the two streams is a bottleneck cross-attention mechanism. It allows the spatial expert and temporal expert to exchange information, so their predictions can draw on each other’s understanding. The architecture therefore gives each stream a distinct role while explicitly providing a way to coordinate those roles during recognition.

The authors evaluate CAST on EPIC-Kitchens-100, Something-Something-V2, and Kinetics-400, benchmarks with different characteristics. They report consistently favorable performance across all three, whereas existing methods vary more with the dataset. This pattern supports the value of balanced spatial and temporal processing: exchanging information between experts helps the model perform well across the evaluated video settings, without requiring input beyond RGB.
neurips-2023-cast-cross-attention-in-spa.tldr: CAST lets spatial and temporal video experts exchange information through cross-attention, producing consistently favorable action-recognition results across three benchmarks.

paragraphs: Adapting a text-to-image diffusion model requires changing its behavior while preserving the useful generation capabilities it already has. Orthogonal Finetuning, or OFT, approaches this through a geometric constraint on the model’s neurons. The paper focuses on preserving relationships within the network as it learns a downstream task.

OFT provably preserves hyperspherical energy, a quantity describing pairwise neuron relationships on a unit hypersphere. The authors find that this preservation is crucial for retaining semantic generation ability. They also introduce Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning, which adds a radius constraint to improve the stability of the adaptation process.

The method is studied in two settings: learning to generate a particular subject from a few example images and a text prompt, and enabling generation with additional control signals. In the reported experiments, OFT improves generation quality and convergence speed over existing methods. The geometric preservation is a formal property of the method; its benefits for generation are supported by the empirical comparisons in these adaptation tasks.
neurips-2023-controlling-text-to-image-d.tldr: Orthogonal Finetuning preserves a geometric measure of neuron relationships while adapting diffusion models, improving reported generation quality and convergence speed.

paragraphs: Described Object Detection asks a detector to find objects using language that can range from a short category name to a detailed description. It broadens open-vocabulary detection and removes the referring-expression assumption that the described object is already present. The task must therefore handle absent matches as well as multiple matching objects.

The authors introduce the Description Detection Dataset, D³, with annotations covering all described objects across all images. Evaluating existing methods exposes different weaknesses: referring-expression systems struggle with confidence scores, negative instances, and multiple targets, while open-vocabulary detectors struggle with long, complex descriptions. Methods supporting both tasks also perform poorly when their training and inference remain separated.

The paper then develops a baseline that restructures training data and adds a binary classification subtask to improve referring-expression methods. It outperforms the existing methods in the reported evaluation. Together, the dataset and baseline make flexible language-driven detection more concrete, showing why recognizing a named category or locating one assumed-present object does not fully address this broader task.
neurips-2023-described-object-detection-.tldr: The paper introduces flexible description-based object detection, a comprehensively annotated dataset, and an improved baseline for handling absent or multiple matches.

paragraphs: A partial 3D observation can be consistent with several complete objects, so shape completion naturally admits multiple plausible answers. Producing that variety can express uncertainty about unseen regions and could benefit downstream planning. This paper develops a conditional generative adversarial network that produces diverse completions of the same partially observed point cloud.

The network introduces randomness through style modulation. During training, it extracts style codes from complete shapes and learns a distribution over those codes. Because the codes can explicitly carry shape-category information, varying them can guide different completions while preserving information useful for reconstructing a plausible full object.

The training design also uses diversity penalties and discriminators operating at multiple scales to prevent conditional mode collapse, where different random inputs lead to essentially the same completion. It does not require multiple ground-truth completions for each partial input. Across synthetic and real datasets, the authors report greater diversity alongside better respect for observed geometry, supporting the joint pursuit of variation and consistency.
neurips-2023-diverse-shape-completion-vi.tldr: A style-modulated generative network produces more diverse 3D shape completions while better preserving observed geometry, without multiple reference completions per input.

paragraphs: Differentially private learning commonly relies on gradient descent, which uses first-order information about a loss function. Second-order methods also use information about its curvature and can converge faster without privacy constraints. This paper investigates whether those advantages can be retained when the optimization procedure must provide differential privacy.

The theoretical contribution is a private version of a regularized cubic Newton method. For strongly convex loss functions, the authors establish quadratic convergence and optimal excess loss. These guarantees are tied to that stated function class, giving a specific setting in which second-order information can accelerate private optimization while retaining a strong accuracy guarantee.

The authors also design a practical second-order private algorithm for unconstrained logistic regression and analyze it theoretically and empirically. In their experiments, it consistently achieves the best excess loss among the compared baselines and runs 10–40 times faster than private gradient-descent methods on challenging datasets. The work connects a formal result for strongly convex objectives with evidence of substantial practical gains in logistic regression.
neurips-2023-faster-differentially-priva.tldr: Private second-order optimization achieves strong guarantees for strongly convex losses and substantial reported speedups for unconstrained logistic regression.

paragraphs: Different neural-network parameter settings can implement exactly the same input–output function. The collection of all such settings is a functional equivalence class. Understanding its structure helps describe the parameter space in which learning takes place. This paper studies unusually rich equivalence classes created by redundant network units.

The analysis concerns networks with one hidden layer and hyperbolic tangent activations. Although almost all parameters have relatively simple, established equivalence classes, a vanishing minority are reducible because their units contain redundancies. The authors provide an algorithmic characterization of these redundancies and the associated reducible equivalence classes.

They prove that these classes are connected by piecewise-linear paths: equivalent parameter settings can be joined through straight segments while remaining within the same class. When a majority of units are redundant, at most seven such segments are needed. This bound concerns the number of segments, rather than ordinary geometric distance. The findings reveal concrete structure in exceptional parameter configurations that simpler descriptions of typical networks do not capture.
neurips-2023-functional-equivalence-and-.tldr: For single-hidden-layer tanh networks, the paper characterizes redundant parameters and proves their functional equivalence classes have piecewise-linear connecting paths.

paragraphs: Visual prostheses can produce different percepts across individuals because implant placement and perception vary. Personalizing electrical stimulation is difficult: Bayesian optimization struggles with high-dimensional stimuli, while deep encoders typically assume accurate knowledge of the patient. This paper combines the two approaches to personalize an encoder through comparisons between candidate stimuli.

First, a deep network learns to invert a forward model that maps electrical stimulation to visual perception, producing stimuli for different patient-specific settings. Preferential Bayesian optimization then uses this encoder to learn suitable parameters for a new patient. Its feedback takes the form of pairwise preferences, reducing the burden of evaluating candidate stimulation patterns.

The authors demonstrate the approach using a visual-prosthesis model, reporting rapid personalization and large improvements over existing encoding strategies. They also find robustness to noisy feedback and misspecification of the forward model. These model-based results suggest that combining learned stimulus generation with preference-driven adaptation could improve patients’ perceptual experience and may extend to other neuroprosthetic technologies.
neurips-2023-human-in-the-loop-optimizat.tldr: A deep stimulus encoder combined with preference-based Bayesian optimization personalizes visual-prosthesis stimulation and improves percept quality in model-based evaluations.

paragraphs: A short, abstract prompt leaves many visual details unspecified. This paper studies how to turn such prompts into intricate images by explicitly expanding the scene before generating its appearance. The proposed scene-graph hallucination mechanism adds feasible detail to a structured representation of the initial prompt.

The system uses two diffusion processes with different roles. A discrete diffusion module develops the scene graph by repeatedly introducing new scene elements. A continuous-state diffusion model then generates the image under the guidance of that expanded semantic structure. Keeping the imagined content in a scene graph provides a structured basis for controlling how the scene is elaborated.

On COCO, the authors report a significant improvement over the existing best-performing text-to-image model, especially for the abstract-to-intricate setting. The result supports an explicit intermediate stage between a sparse prompt and a detailed image: the system first develops what the scene contains, then uses that representation to direct image synthesis. Additional analyses investigate how the proposed components contribute.
neurips-2023-imagine-that-abstract-to-in.tldr: The system expands simple prompts into detailed scene graphs with discrete diffusion, then uses those graphs to guide image generation.

paragraphs: Cutting planes help solve integer programs by adding valid inequalities that exclude a target point while retaining feasible solutions. Many methods derive these inequalities through explicit rules. Local-cut approaches instead seek the facets, or defining faces, of the relevant polyhedron, but existing approaches rely on solving linear programs to obtain them.

This paper proposes learning those facets through an enumeration oracle that provides implicit access to the polyhedron in a reduced-dimensional setting. The oracle is embedded in a variant of the Frank–Wolfe algorithm. Together, these components generate strong cutting planes, effectively converting the ability to enumerate into the ability to separate a target point.

The authors demonstrate the approach in a case study on the multidimensional knapsack problem. Its broader methodological contribution is the connection between two kinds of access to a feasible region: an enumeration procedure becomes a building block for constructing separating inequalities. The case study provides evidence of effectiveness for that problem, while the proposed construction is presented as a generic approach.
neurips-2023-learning-cuts-via-enumerati.tldr: A Frank–Wolfe variant turns a reduced-dimensional enumeration oracle into a method for learning facets and generating strong integer-programming cuts.

paragraphs: An image can support many correct descriptions, yet standard maximum-likelihood training penalizes a caption whenever it differs from the reference. The paper identifies a conflict within this learning signal. Predictions richer than the label are pushed toward conciseness, while predictions less detailed than the label are pushed toward richer wording.

The authors argue that these opposing pressures can lead models toward general descriptions. Their proposed objective, Semipermeable Maximum Likelihood Estimation, or SMILE, selectively permits the updates that encourage richer expression while blocking those that encourage conciseness. The purpose is to preserve a learning signal for additional detail without automatically suppressing richer predictions merely because the reference is shorter.

Experiments on MSCOCO and Flickr30K show significant improvements in the descriptiveness of generated captions. The method encourages longer captions containing more details, and the paper includes further investigations into its behavior. The contribution is a change in how reference mismatches influence training, addressing the tension between learning from a particular label and recognizing that an image admits multiple valid descriptions.
neurips-2023-learning-descriptive-image-.tldr: SMILE selectively blocks training updates toward conciseness, producing more descriptive image captions in experiments on MSCOCO and Flickr30K.

paragraphs: This paper uses a large language model to construct an explicit description of a planning domain, then hands planning to a dedicated planner. The domain is written in PDDL, a language for specifying planning problems. This separates the work of describing how a world operates from finding a sequence of actions within that description.

Because the initial domain model may contain errors, the language model also mediates corrective feedback from validators and people. It can translate PDDL into natural language for users unfamiliar with the formalism and encode their corrections back into the model. Users can therefore repair a reusable domain description at the beginning instead of repeatedly correcting individual plans.

The framework inherits the correctness guarantees of sound external planners for planning with the supplied model. Across two IPC domains and a more complex Household domain, GPT-4 produces high-quality models covering over 40 actions. After correction, those models solve 48 challenging tasks, demonstrating how an editable world model can support repeated planning while reducing human involvement.
neurips-2023-leveraging-pre-trained-larg.tldr: LLMs build and help correct reusable PDDL world models, enabling sound external planners to solve tasks with less repeated human intervention.

paragraphs: Non-Cartesian grids are useful in areas such as simulation and scientific visualization, yet they have received little attention in machine learning. The paper identifies two practical obstacles: representing data on these domains and providing the operations that learning algorithms expect. NCDL addresses both through a new data structure and supporting software.

The central abstraction is a lattice tensor. It extends the spatial and temporal operations associated with ordinary tensors to data arranged on lattices, making standard machine-learning algorithms usable on non-Cartesian data. The accompanying library implements the container and a set of common operations, giving the representation a practical computational foundation.

The framework also applies when the original data are Cartesian. Non-dyadic downsampling schemes bring those data into a non-Cartesian space for subsequent processing. This makes the approach relevant both to data that naturally use alternative grids and to processing pipelines that introduce them. The authors demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, presenting infrastructure for exploring these domains rather than a single task-specific model.
neurips-2023-ncdl-a-framework-for-deep-l.tldr: NCDL introduces lattice tensors and software operations that support machine learning on non-Cartesian grids, including grids derived from Cartesian data.

paragraphs: In learning with experts, an algorithm predicts repeatedly and compares its accumulated cost with that of the best expert in hindsight. The difficulty increases when earlier predictions influence future inputs. This paper studies how to remain robust to that adaptivity while using limited memory.

The authors give a randomized algorithm with a smooth trade-off between memory and regret. For n experts over T rounds, its space scales as n divided by R times the square root of T, up to polylogarithmic factors, under a stated bound on the best expert’s mistakes. Thus, the guarantee explicitly connects memory use, tolerated regret, and the difficulty of the prediction sequence.

They also establish a memory lower bound for randomized algorithms achieving the target regret with an extremely high success probability. This implies that a natural deterministic procedure cycling through pools of experts is optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. Experiments additionally demonstrate benefits of robust procedures against an adversary that can inspect internal state, complementing the theoretical trade-offs with an adversarial evaluation.
neurips-2023-on-robust-streaming-for-lea.tldr: The paper develops memory-efficient expert-learning algorithms for adaptive inputs and proves conditional lower bounds on the memory needed for robust performance.

paragraphs: Randomized classifiers have been proposed as defenses against small adversarial changes to test inputs, but findings about their effectiveness have conflicted. This paper clarifies the comparison by distinguishing between a fixed family of deterministic classifiers and the broader collection of deterministic classifiers that might be considered.

For a given base hypothesis set, the authors establish conditions under which a randomized ensemble achieves lower adversarial risk than that set. Randomization can therefore improve on the available base classifiers under those conditions. Separately, they prove that every probabilistic binary classifier has a deterministic classifier that outperforms it, including when the probabilistic classifier is a randomized ensemble.

These statements concern different comparison sets, which explains how both can hold. Beating the original family does not establish an advantage over all deterministic classifiers. The paper also explicitly describes a deterministic hypothesis set containing such a better classifier for common randomization schemes, including ensembles and parameter or input noise. The result sharpens what a claimed robustness benefit from randomization actually establishes.
neurips-2023-on-the-role-of-randomizatio.tldr: Randomization can beat a fixed base family under stated conditions, yet every probabilistic binary classifier has a better deterministic counterpart.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using guidance from a teacher. Many methods assume that both models belong to the same architectural family, especially when the student is asked to match intermediate features. This paper examines what happens when teacher and student use different architectures.

Using centered kernel alignment, the authors observe substantial divergence between the features learned by heterogeneous models. OFA-KD addresses that mismatch by projecting intermediate features into an aligned latent space, such as the logits space, where architecture-specific information is discarded. An adaptive target-enhancement scheme further reduces interference from information irrelevant to the student.

Experiments span convolutional networks, Transformers, and multilayer perceptrons. The authors report improved cross-architecture distillation, with maximum student gains of 8.0% on CIFAR-100 and 0.7% on ImageNet-1K. These findings support aligning what the models communicate before transferring knowledge: directly matching internal features can be ineffective when those features reflect fundamentally different architectural representations.
neurips-2023-one-for-all-bridge-the-gap-.tldr: OFA-KD aligns teacher and student features in a shared space to improve knowledge transfer between different neural-network architectures.

paragraphs: LiDAR detectors can process a compact range image efficiently with two-dimensional convolutions, but range-view methods have trailed bird’s-eye-view approaches in accuracy. RangePerception seeks to close that gap while preserving efficient processing. Its design follows an analysis of two problems in the range-view representation.

The first is a mismatch between the two-dimensional coordinates of the input range image and the three-dimensional world coordinates required for detection. The second is visual corruption affecting objects near the range image’s margins. The proposed Range Aware Kernel and Vision Restoration Module address these obstacles and help connect the range representation to 3D detection outputs.

On the Waymo Open Dataset, RangePerception improves averaged L1 and L2 average precision over RangeDet by 3.25 and 4.18, respectively. It also achieves slightly higher averaged average precision than the bird’s-eye-view detector CenterPoint while running inference 1.3 times as fast. These comparisons support the claim that addressing representation-specific problems can improve range-view accuracy without giving up its efficiency advantage.
neurips-2023-rangeperception-taming-lida.tldr: RangePerception addresses coordinate mismatch and image-margin corruption to improve range-view LiDAR detection, slightly exceeding CenterPoint’s reported accuracy with faster inference.

paragraphs: Coupling normalizing flows offer fast sampling and density evaluation, but their standard architecture obstructs the symmetries needed when modeling atomic coordinates. This paper introduces a flow that preserves equivariance under rotations, translations, and atom permutations while retaining those computational advantages.

The method performs coordinate splits along extra, augmented dimensions. Each layer maps atomic positions into learned invariant bases, applies standard flow transformations there, and returns to the original basis. The resulting model can also support unbiased estimates of target-distribution expectations through importance sampling, connecting efficient generation with a way to estimate physical quantities.

On DW4, LJ13, and QM9-positional data, the flow is competitive with equivariant continuous flows and diffusion models while sampling more than an order of magnitude faster. The authors also report learning alanine dipeptide’s full Boltzmann distribution using only Cartesian atomic positions, a first to their knowledge. For DW4 and LJ13, they demonstrate approximate Boltzmann sampling learned directly from energy functions.
neurips-2023-se-3-equivariant-augmented-.tldr: Augmented coupling flows preserve physical symmetries while enabling fast sampling and density evaluation for atomic systems.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes are widely used to guide Bayesian optimization and active learning, but their effectiveness depends heavily on suitable hyperparameters. This paper treats learning those settings as an explicit objective when selecting new observations. The aim is to improve the model while using it to learn or optimize.

Statistical distance-based Active Learning, or SAL, chooses observations using the average disagreement among posterior samples, measured through a statistical distance. This explicitly prioritizes hyperparameter learning. Self-Correcting Bayesian Optimization, or SCoreBO, extends that idea so that active learning and objective optimization take place together.

The authors report that SAL outperforms leading active-learning methods on several test functions. SCoreBO learns hyperparameters faster than vanilla Bayesian optimization and outperforms recent optimization methods on traditional benchmarks. Further experiments on atypical optimization tasks demonstrate the importance of self-correction. Together, the findings support choosing observations partly for their ability to improve the model’s own settings, rather than assuming those settings are already adequate for effective search.
neurips-2023-self-correcting-bayesian-op.tldr: SAL and SCoreBO select observations that explicitly improve Gaussian-process hyperparameters, strengthening active learning and Bayesian optimization in reported experiments.

paragraphs: For models of molecules and materials, predictive accuracy alone may not ensure physically sensible behavior. Smoothness and the correct response to translations, rotations, and permutations of identical atoms also matter. Architectures designed to enforce these requirements can restrict the range of model designs available to researchers.

The paper proposes a general symmetrization method that adds exact rotational equivariance to a given model while preserving the other requirements. Equivariance means that rotating the input produces the corresponding transformation of the output. This allows researchers to draw on more varied point-cloud architectures while supplying rotational behavior through a separate protocol.

The authors demonstrate the idea with the Point Edge Transformer, or PET. Although PET is not intrinsically equivariant, it achieves state-of-the-art results on several molecular and solid-state benchmarks. Applying the symmetrization protocol afterward makes it exactly equivariant with minimal changes to accuracy. The contribution therefore connects architectural flexibility with rigorous symmetry requirements that are important for usable atomic-scale models.
neurips-2023-smooth-exact-rotational-sym.tldr: A general symmetrization protocol adds exact rotational equivariance while preserving other physical requirements, demonstrated on the accurate Point Edge Transformer.

paragraphs: Molecular transitions between metastable states can be rare in ordinary molecular dynamics because high energy barriers separate the states. Traditional methods increase transition frequency using a bias potential guided by collective variables, a reduced description of the system. Choosing suitable variables requires chemical intuition and becomes difficult for larger systems.

Poorly chosen collective variables can direct the bias along dimensions irrelevant to the transition. This paper develops PIPS, a machine-learning method that avoids requiring those variables. Its foundation is a formal relationship between transition-path sampling, the Schrödinger bridge problem, and stochastic optimal control with neural-network policies.

The authors demonstrate that PIPS generates low-energy transitions for alanine dipeptide and for the larger polyproline and chignolin proteins. These results support learning how to guide molecular transitions without first hand-selecting a reduced set of collective variables. The theoretical connection supplies the basis for the method, while the molecular examples show its ability to produce transitions across the systems studied.
neurips-2023-stochastic-optimal-control-.tldr: PIPS uses neural stochastic optimal control to sample molecular transition paths without hand-selected collective variables.

paragraphs: Language-model training commonly mixes filtered web pages with curated sources such as books, conversations, and technical papers. Such curation has been viewed as necessary for strong performance and broad zero-shot generalization. This paper questions that assumption as training requirements grow to trillions of tokens and curated data become harder to scale.

The authors show that web data alone can support powerful models when it is carefully filtered and deduplicated. In their comparisons, models trained this way significantly outperform models trained on The Pile. The claim depends on the quality of the processing: the contribution centers on making a large web collection suitable for training.

Even after extensive filtering, the authors obtain five trillion tokens from CommonCrawl. They release a 500-billion-token portion of RefinedWeb and language models with 1.3 billion and 7.5 billion parameters trained on it. The findings indicate that well-processed web data can provide both substantial scale and strong model performance, challenging the presumed necessity of adding curated corpora.
neurips-2023-the-refinedweb-dataset-for-.tldr: RefinedWeb shows that carefully filtered and deduplicated web data alone can train strong language models while remaining available at trillion-token scale.
